sample_data.reset_instructions: Judged path needs no reset: POST /api/run is stateless, unauthenticated, takes a whole case in the request body and never touches the database, so every call starts from the data supplied. The published case PUB-01 ships at src/data/case-pub-01.json and `npx tsx src/lib/engine-check.ts` reproduces the documented answers from it offline. The signed-in workshop app reads from PostgreSQL, which was seeded out of band from the 25-case public drop (P09_vehicle_service_public.json); that file is not committed and no seed script exists, so the database cannot currently be rebuilt from a clone. See known_limitations.

problem_solving_method: All domain calculation lives in one pure, I/O-free module (src/lib/engine.ts) that takes the published case shape and returns per-item status, the ranked call list and the 8-week workload. `today` is a field on the case, never the system clock, so results are deterministic and reproducible. PostgreSQL stores the same shape and src/lib/case-db.ts serialises it back byte-identical to the published file, so the engine, the UI and the self-check run unchanged over either source — src/lib/engine-check.ts asserts the documented PUB-01 answers against both the JSON fixture and the database-assembled case, and any drift in the persistence layer shows up as a wrong number rather than a subtly wrong ordering. Two separate, optional Python models (ml/) answer the behavioural half — when an owner will actually turn up, and the probability they turn up on their own — which is a different question from when work is due; they are treated as an optimisation, not a dependency, and /api/visit falls back to a committed lookup table whenever the model service is unreachable. Module-by-module documentation is in docs/.

R1.evidence: 25 published cases in PostgreSQL, each 27 owners and 42 vehicles with 3-5 service items (all three rules), 2-4 odometer readings and past service records — 1,052 vehicles, 677 owners, 4,197 service items and 2,600 distinct visits as they stand, growing as customers are entered through the app. Schema in prisma/schema.prisma (Case, Owner, Vehicle, OdometerReading, ServiceItem, ServiceRecord); assembly in src/lib/case-db.ts; offline fixture at src/data/case-pub-01.json. New customers, vehicles and service items can also be entered in the app: src/components/due-book/intake-form.tsx, POST /api/vehicle and POST /api/service-item, backed by intakeVehicle() / addServiceItem() in src/lib/case-db.ts.

R2.evidence: src/lib/engine.ts computeItem() implements all three rules — fixed_date reads the printed expiry; period_months adds calendar months to the last service, clamped to month end (31 Jan + 1 month = 28 Feb); distance_km projects the due date from last-service odometer + every_km divided by kmPerDay(), derived from that vehicle's own reading history, with a fleet-median fallback for single-reading vehicles and a zero-rate guard that never divides. Every item is classified overdue / due_soon / fine. Verified by src/lib/engine-check.ts, which reproduces the documented PUB-01 answers exactly from both the file and the database: top-6 call list (V28 117,690 down to V07 64,000), backlog 45 jobs / 387,700, and the eight weekly buckets.

R3.evidence: Daily call list at /dashboard (src/components/due-book/call-list.tsx), one row per owner+vehicle with name, phone, model, plate, the due items and a plain-English reason for each date. Ranked by score = cost x urgency x safety weight summed over the vehicle's items, so lateness and value are combined; the arithmetic behind each row is printed (e.g. '32,000 x 1.97 x 1.5 = 94,400 + 19,250 + 4,040') so any position is defensible. Sort modes: score (default), most overdue, highest value. buildCallList() in src/lib/engine.ts.

R4.evidence: Vehicle page (src/components/due-book/vehicle-detail.tsx) lists every service item with its next due date, status, cost and the reason for that date, plus odometer, km/day and service history. 'Record a completed service' appends a history row and resets that one item — POST /api/service to recordServiceDb() in src/lib/case-db.ts — and the page then names the item whose next-due date moved and counts the ones that did not, so the one-item reset guarantee is shown on screen rather than assumed. Odometer re-entry (POST /api/odometer) upserts the reading dated `today` and every distance-based estimate on the vehicle recomputes; a reading that goes backwards or implies more than 3x the vehicle's own km/day is rejected with the offending number named, so a mistyped digit cannot silently poison every distance estimate on the car.

beyond_requirements: 8-week workload forecast with a per-week job list (src/components/due-book/workload.tsx).
Copy-ready reminder message per owner, merged across their vehicles, plus a wa.me deep link that opens WhatsApp with the message already typed — no WhatsApp Business account or API involved.
Search across customer name, phone, plate, model and vehicle id, grouped by customer (src/components/due-book/search.tsx).
Method page that shows how every number on the screen is derived, including a worked example of the top-ranked vehicle.
Adjustable due-soon window (14/30/45 days), km/day basis (all readings or last two) and safety weighting on/off, so the ranking rule can be interrogated live.

Next-visit prediction: a random forest over 1,549 observed inter-visit gaps from 1,052 vehicles across all 25 workshops predicts when an owner actually returns — MAE 41.5 days against a 62.5-day baseline under leave-one-CASE-out validation, with 0 of 12 shuffled-label refits beating it — and flags the vehicles that are due but will not come back on their own (ml/visit_model.py, src/lib/visit.ts, POST /api/visit).

Return probability: a discrete-time hazard over 9,952 person-periods, fitted on the 1,549 completed gaps AND the 1,051 still-open spells the point model has to discard, answers 'will they turn up on their own in the next 30/60 days?'. Leave-one-case-out Brier 0.12583 against 0.13143 for the flat fleet rate; the calibration is the result (0.344 predicted -> 0.323 observed). ml/return_model.py, exposed on POST /api/visit.
Offline case runner: `npm run cases -- <file>` answers one or more case files with no browser and no database, byte-identical to POST /api/run because both call the same buildAnswers().
Multi-user auth with each account pinned to one workshop; the workshop is read from the session on every request and never from the query string or body.
Module-by-module documentation in docs/ — architecture, domain engine, data model, API reference, auth, UI, the ML pipeline, verification, operations and a glossary.

Workshop accounts: User.role (manager | staff — not 'owner', which in this schema is the customer), a manager adds colleagues from the dashboard with caseId taken from the session rather than the form, anyone can change their own password, and User.passwordChangedAt compared against the JWT's iat retires every session issued before the change, so whoever was told the starting password stops being signed in the moment it is changed (src/lib/auth.ts, src/actions/auth.action.ts, src/components/account/account.tsx).

major_design_decisions: `today` is a field on the case, not the system clock — no new Date() in the engine, so every due date, status and ranking is deterministic and reproducible by judges.
All domain calculation sits in one pure module (src/lib/engine.ts) with no I/O, so it is testable without a database and runs identically over the JSON fixture or the PostgreSQL rows.

Distance-based items are projected from each vehicle's own km/day, computed from its odometer history, with a fleet-median fallback for a single reading and a zero-rate guard that reports 'cannot come due' instead of dividing.
An item with no service history counts from the odometer reading on the clock, not from zero — otherwise a newly entered car reads thousands of days overdue and heads the call list.

Dates are stored as plain ISO strings and money as Decimal(10,2) serialised with toFixed(2), so the assembled case is byte-identical to the published fixture and no timezone bug can enter through SQL.
Vehicle and owner ids are unique only within a case, so caseId is part of every primary key, unique constraint and foreign key, and every query is scoped by it.

A signed-in user works out of exactly one workshop, read from the session on every request and never accepted from the client, so no account can read or write another workshop's data by changing a parameter.

Service items are chosen from a closed catalogue of the twelve services the published data contains, never typed: the safety weighting matches on the item name, so a typed 'Tyre' would silently lose the 1.5x weight and rank the car too low with no error anywhere.

The ML service is an optimisation, not a dependency — /api/visit answers from a committed lookup table whenever the model is unreachable, and reports which source it used, so a dropped tunnel degrades visibly instead of breaking the demo.

WhatsApp reminders are a wa.me deep link rather than an API integration: the workshop reviews the message and sends it themselves, and the app needs no Business account, token or outbound messaging permission.

Every vehicle's current absence is right-censored — they have not come back yet — so the visit model clamps its prediction to today rather than predicting backwards, and the return-probability model is fitted on person-period rows so those 1,051 open spells count as evidence instead of being discarded.

The return-probability model's tail is held flat past 270 days, where fewer than 40 spells are still at risk: uncapped it read 0.692, 0.875 and then 1.000 off a single spell, telling the workshop a long-absent customer was certain to return — the exact opposite of what a long absence means.

The ranking change the return probability was built for is specified (ml/RETURN-HANDOFF.md) and deliberately not landed: it must arrive as a fourth EngineOpts knob defaulting off, because switching it on by default would break the engine-check fixtures that are the reason anyone believes the call list.
known_limitations: The database cannot be rebuilt from a clone: the 25-case public drop is not committed and there is no seed script, so a fresh environment can run /api/run and the offline self-check but not the signed-in workshop app without re-seeding by hand.

PUB-01 is the pinned fixture that engine-check asserts against, so recording a service against it through the UI would invalidate that check; user accounts are deliberately pinned to other cases to prevent this.
The visit model's 80% interval is roughly +/-65 days (p10 -67, p90 +63). The point date is far less useful than the probability, which is why the return-probability model exists.

The return-probability model beats the flat fleet rate by 4.3% of Brier score — a modest gain. Its calibration is the real result, and per-vehicle features (km/day, item count, annual burden) were tried and did not beat the bare hazard table, so the table is what ships.
The return probability is exposed on POST /api/visit but does not yet change the call-list ranking or appear as a chip on screen; the change is specified in ml/RETURN-HANDOFF.md.

The model service runs behind a free-tier ngrok tunnel whose URL changes on every restart; when it is stale the app silently uses the committed table, which is visible in the UI as 'offline model' and in the response as source: 'bundled'.

A workshop outside the model's training set falls back to the fleet median and says so in `basis`, because per-vehicle curves differ by more than the model's own error and reusing one case's curve on another would be a confident wrong answer.

There is no edit or delete for customers, vehicles or service items. A manager can add a colleague but not remove one, change their role or reset their password; that still needs a database statement, and doing it properly needs a last-manager guard. The first manager of a workshop is also assigned by hand — there is no bootstrap flow, and public registration is still open although it grants nothing.

Verification is assert-based self-checks (src/lib/engine-check.ts, src/lib/visit-check.ts, and the check() blocks in ml/visit_model.py and ml/return_model.py) run manually, not a test framework suite wired into CI.

A colleague's starting password is set by the manager and shown on screen so it can be read out; there is no forced change on first login and no email invitation. The colleague changing it is what locks the manager out of their account. There is no rate limiting on login or on the change-password action.

ai_tools_used.used_for: Reconciling the Prisma schema with the already-seeded database; the case assembly and write layer; the API routes; the dashboard UI ported from a hand-authored design mockup; walk-in customer and vehicle intake; per-account workshop scoping; the visit-prediction and return-probability pipelines; the workshop account system (roles, adding staff, changing a password, retiring stale sessions); and the module documentation in docs/.
ai_tools_used.how_output_was_verified: src/lib/engine-check.ts reproduces the documented PUB-01 answers (top-6 call-list scores, 45-job / 387,700 backlog, eight weekly buckets) from both the JSON fixture and the database-assembled case, so any drift surfaces as a wrong number. src/lib/visit-check.ts asserts the model never predicts a visit in the past, never falls outside its own interval, moves when a service is recorded, and that the TypeScript and Python copies of the return-probability formula agree to 1e-3 across all 42 vehicles. Both Python models assert their own claims on every training run — model beats baseline, 0 of 12 shuffled-label refits match it, no hazard reaches certainty. `prisma migrate diff` was used to confirm the schema matches the live database with an empty diff in both directions. Each feature was then exercised in a real browser against the running app — intake, recording a service, the odometer update, search and the visit prediction — and checked against the database rows and the /api/run response rather than assumed. `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx biome check` and `npx next build` pass.
